title: CDC and event-driven pipelines
summary: Change data capture and storage events push changes to you in seconds. Delivery is at least once and unordered, so the pipeline must treat events as hints and write idempotently.
useIf: Freshness must be seconds, the source emits changes (change feed, database log, storage events) and you can run a queue and workers.
avoidIf: Hourly freshness is enough and a supported indexer exists: events add operational burden with no business gain.

explain.md: Three event sources are common. The **Cosmos DB change feed** has two modes. Latest version mode records creates and updates, keeps only the newest change per item and does not capture deletes (use a soft-delete flag plus TTL). All versions and deletes mode records every create, update and delete in order, but it needs continuous backup, an opt-in flag, and can be read only within the backup retention window [[tr23]]. **Blob events** flow through Event Grid [[tr24]]. **Debezium** reads the database log and emits a delete event followed, for Kafka compaction, by a tombstone with a null value [[tr25]].

None of them promises exactly once. Event Grid tries to deliver each event at least once, does not guarantee order, and retries on a schedule that starts at 10 seconds and backs off to every 12 hours up to 24 hours. The defaults are 30 attempts and a 1,440 minute time to live, and a failed event is dead-lettered only if you configured that [[tr26]]. Debezium can emit duplicates after a fault [[tr25]]. Items in one Cosmos DB transactional batch share a modification time and may arrive in any order [[tr23]].

The practical answer is **effectively once**: at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent sink. Treat each event as a notification that item X changed. The worker re-reads the current state from the source, builds a stable key from the source id, and writes with `mergeOrUpload`. Re-reading makes stale and out-of-order events harmless, because the worker always indexes the latest state.

explain.title: Event as a hint, source as the truth
explain.alt: The source emits a change event to Event Grid, which delivers it to a worker. The worker reads current state from the source, upserts to the index with a stable key and acknowledges the event.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Source
  participant E as Event Grid
  participant W as Worker
  participant X as Index
  S->>E: change event
  E->>W: deliver, at least once
  W->>S: read current state
  W->>X: mergeOrUpload with stable key
  W-->>E: acknowledge

explain.title: Large blobs fire early
explain.md: To fire `BlobCreated` only after a block blob is fully committed, filter on the `CopyBlob`, `PutBlob`, `PutBlockList` or `FlushWithClose` calls [[tr24]].

whereToUse: Searchable tickets, chat or order data that must be fresh within seconds
Cosmos DB backed applications that need search updates driven by the change feed
Blob uploads that trigger parsing and indexing through Event Grid
Relational databases streamed through log-based CDC such as Debezium into a queue
Pipelines that need replay, dead-letter handling and per-item observability

use: Use events when the freshness target is seconds and the source can emit changes
Use all versions and deletes mode when hard deletes must be seen and continuous backup is available
Use re-read-on-event so ordering mistakes cannot overwrite new data with old
Use a dead-letter destination and alert on its depth
avoid: Avoid assuming exactly-once delivery or global ordering
Avoid latest version change feed alone when deletes matter and you cannot add a soft-delete flag
Avoid running an event pipeline for a corpus that changes nightly
flips: Freshness relaxes to 15 minutes or more: a GA indexer is cheaper to run
Hard deletes must be visible and continuous backup is off: add soft delete plus TTL or reconcile on a schedule
Events must be replayed after a bug: keep source state re-readable and key writes by stable id

pitfalls.symptom: Old data overwrites newer data in the index
pitfalls.cause: Events arrived out of order and the worker indexed the event payload
pitfalls.fix: Re-read current state from the source or compare a version number before writing

pitfalls.symptom: Duplicate chunks or double work after a failure
pitfalls.cause: At-least-once delivery from Event Grid or Debezium with a random key per attempt
pitfalls.fix: Derive keys from source id and position, and upsert

pitfalls.symptom: Deleted Cosmos DB items stay searchable
pitfalls.cause: Latest version mode does not capture deletes
pitfalls.fix: Use a soft-delete flag plus TTL, or all versions and deletes mode where the prerequisites hold

pitfalls.cause: Retries ended at 30 attempts or 1,440 minutes with no dead-letter destination
pitfalls.fix: Configure dead-lettering and a replay procedure

scenarios.title: Hard deletes in a Cosmos DB catalogue
scenarios.situation: A product catalogue in Cosmos DB feeds search. The application hard-deletes retired products and the code cannot change this quarter. Continuous backup is enabled and the consumer keeps up within minutes.
constraints: Hard deletes must reach the index
unknowns: How long is the continuous backup retention?
Can the consumer fall behind for days?
scenarios.question: How do you propagate deletes?

options.name: Read the change feed in all versions and deletes mode
options.why: It records deletes in order, and the prerequisites hold here.
options.tradeoff: Opt-in feature, readable only within the backup retention window, and starts only from now or a checkpoint.

options.name: Latest version mode plus a nightly id reconciliation
options.why: Works without extra prerequisites and catches deletes eventually.
options.tradeoff: Deleted products stay searchable until the next reconciliation.

options.name: Indexer on `_ts` with default settings
options.why: Hard deletes are invisible to the indexer.
options.tradeoff: Right when the app uses a Boolean soft-delete field.

flips.then: Use latest version mode plus reconciliation, or change the app to soft delete.
Soft delete plus TTL with the indexer is simplest.

scenarios.takeaway: Decide how deletes reach you before you choose the event source.

scenarios.title: Large uploads into Blob Storage
scenarios.situation: Users upload large files in many blocks. A worker is triggered per event. Sometimes it reads a half-written file or processes the same file twice.
unknowns: What does the worker do on a partial read?
scenarios.question: What do you change?

options.name: Filter events to completion calls, make the worker idempotent, and enable dead-lettering
options.why: It fixes early events at the source and makes duplicates harmless.
options.tradeoff: A little setup and a stable-key convention.

options.name: Add a fixed 10 minute delay before processing
options.why: It guesses at upload time, still allows duplicates and delays every file.

options.name: Retry the whole job whenever a read fails
options.tradeoff: Repeats expensive parsing and does not stop duplicates.

flips.then: Early events are rare and idempotency alone suffices.
Switch to an indexer and drop the event path.

scenarios.takeaway: Fix early events at the filter and duplicates in the sink.

quiz.q: What does Debezium guarantee about delivery?
options: At least once, so duplicates can appear after a fault
quiz.explain: Debezium delivers at least once and may emit duplicates after a fault, so consumers should be idempotent. It does not promise exactly once or global ordering.

quiz.q: Which statements about Cosmos DB change feed modes are correct?
options: Latest version mode does not capture deletes
All versions and deletes mode needs continuous backup and an opt-in feature flag
All versions and deletes mode can start from the beginning of time
Latest version mode keeps only the most recent change per item
quiz.explain: Latest version drops deletes and intermediate changes. All versions and deletes needs continuous backup and can start only from now or a checkpoint, within the retention window.

quiz.q: Stale data keeps replacing fresh data in the index. Events are consumed in parallel. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Re-read current source state on each event, or compare a version before writing
quiz.explain: Ordering is not guaranteed, so you must make order irrelevant by indexing current state or comparing versions. Queue size, retry count and dead-lettering do not fix ordering.

flashcards.front: Event Grid delivery guarantees and defaults?
flashcards.back: At least once, no ordering guarantee. Defaults: 30 attempts and 1,440 minute event TTL. Dead-letter only if configured.
At-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent sink, such as a stable key and `mergeOrUpload`.

flashcards.front: Why re-read the source on each change event?
flashcards.back: Events can be duplicated or out of order. Indexing current state makes stale events harmless.
